controllingAuthority.summary: On a not-guilty verdict by judge or jury on all counts, the presiding judge must ask the acquitted person whether they want the records removed and destroyed, and if the answer is yes the court issues the order immediately with no separate petition. The section was renumbered by Public Chapter 268 of 2025, effective 2025-04-24: the acquittal ground that sat at former § 40-32-101(a) is now within § 40-32-106, whose non-conviction grounds include a verdict of not guilty, and which carries the acquittal-in-open-court procedure. No fee may be charged: § 40-32-106(a)(1) provides that qualifying public records must be removed and destroyed without cost to the person. Under § 40-32-110 expunction restores the person, in contemplation of law, to the status occupied before arrest, indictment, information, trial and conviction.

exclusions: A partial acquittal. The immediate route runs on a not-guilty verdict on all counts; a mixed-count case routes to the redaction analysis instead.
A person who was never asked at the verdict, or who declined at the time and later changed their mind. That person routes to the non-conviction petition track, which remains open.
This track offers no participant filing. The order issues in open court on the judge's own question.

controllingAuthority.summary: Created by Public Chapter 268 of 2025, effective 2025-04-24, and codified by Public Chapter 608 effective 2026-03-25. All public records of a person charged with a misdemeanour or felony must, upon petition by that person to the court having jurisdiction in the previous action, be removed and destroyed without cost to the person where the charge was dismissed other than by diversion completion, a no true bill was returned, the person was arrested and released without being charged, a nolle prosequi was entered, a verdict of not guilty was returned, or on the section's further grounds including qualifying implied-consent dismissals, abatement by death, mistaken identity and racial-justice-protest convictions. Subsection (a)(2) extends the same no-cost treatment to a successfully defended order of protection and to expired bonds under § 38-3-109. There is no waiting period. The TBI certificate under § 40-32-102(c) is not required for a § 40-32-106 expunction unless the expunction resulted from successful completion of pretrial or judicial diversion. Under § 40-32-110 expunction restores the person, in contemplation of law, to the status occupied before arrest, indictment, information, trial and conviction, and under § 40-32-102(e) the expunged records are confidential and unlawful release is a Class A misdemeanour.

exclusions: A dismissal that resulted from successful completion of a diversion programme, which routes to the pretrial or judicial diversion tracks and carries a clerk's fee rather than being free.
Any count in the case that resulted in a conviction. A mixed-count case routes to the redaction analysis.
Records in a county other than the one where the case originated, which require a separate filing in each county.

An arrest for which the court with jurisdiction has no history within its records. Section 40-32-106 cannot reach it, because this petition runs to the court having jurisdiction in the previous action and there is no previous action in that court's records. That participant routes to tn_arrest_no_court_record under T.C.A. § 40-32-109, which is a different vehicle and is not free.

components.notes: A controlled petition for expunction of public records drafted to T.C.A. § 40-32-106(a), identifying the court, the docket, the charge, the disposition and the ground relied on, stating the state control number from the TBI history, and requesting removal and destruction of all public records without cost. Tennessee publishes no participant expunction form: confirmed on 2026-08-06 by direct inspection of both AOC form indices. The statute supplies the court, the vehicle, the grounds and the relief, which is what makes a controlled pleading supportable.

States on the face of the packet that this route is free: § 40-32-106(a)(1) requires the records to be removed and destroyed without cost to the person. A participant asked for a fee on this route should query it with the clerk.

Explains where to file and that a separate filing is needed in each county; that expunction is not automatic and the record stays visible until the petition is filed; that no TBI certificate is required on this route unless the case came through diversion; and what happens after the order. A court ordering expunction shall send a copy of the order to the TBI within 30 days for entry into its expunged offender and pretrial diversion database. The order must contain the person's name, date of birth, social security number, the offence dismissed, the state control number referenced in § 8-4-115, the date and cause of dismissal, and the date the order was entered. Nothing changes on a background check until the order reaches the TBI, and the packet tells the participant to confirm that it did. Also explains the § 40-6-204(b) right the participant was supposed to be told about at charging.

Distinguishes the two mechanisms before anything is prepared, because they are not interchangeable. This § 40-32-106 route is free: subsection (a)(1) requires the qualifying records to be removed and destroyed without cost to the person. Where the court with jurisdiction has no history of the arrest within its records, the route is instead T.C.A. § 40-32-109 and the participant goes to tn_arrest_no_court_record, where § 40-32-109(e) makes a clerk's fee mandatory and no waiver provision exists. Section 40-32-109 also carries a step this route does not have at all: under § 40-32-109(c) the clerk's office searches the court's records and certifies to the court whether there is any history of the arrest. That clerk search and certification is required only on the § 40-32-109 route, is the clerk's own instrument, and is never generated or pre-completed. Whether a prior court action ever existed is not something LegalEase adjudicates: the participant answers from their own knowledge, and on the § 40-32-109 route the clerk searches and the court finds.

controllingAuthority.summary: Expunction of the arrest record, with the § 40-32-110 effect expressly applied by § 40-32-109(f): the petitioner is entitled to have all public records destroyed, is restored in contemplation of law to the status occupied before the arrest, must not suffer adverse effects or collateral disabilities by virtue of the offence, and is not guilty of perjury for failing to acknowledge the arrest in response to any inquiry. A person whose arrest record exists but for whom the court with jurisdiction over the offence for which the person was arrested has no history of the arrest within the court's records. This is the participant whose arrest never produced a court file — the case that the § 40-32-106 route cannot reach, because that route runs to the court having jurisdiction in the previous action and here there is no previous action in that court's records. This is the only one of the four additions that does NOT run through § 40-32-108, and it is the only Tennessee route in the entire chapter on which the participant writes the operative petition. Section 40-32-109 contains no cross-reference to § 40-32-108 of any kind, so § 40-32-108(e) — under which the office of the district attorney general must prepare the petition and proposed order — does not reach it. It also carries no waiting period, no 61-day pre-order clock, no rebuttable presumption and no two-year refiling bar, all of which live in § 40-32-108 alone. Section 40-32-109(a) uses the permissive 'may petition', where § 40-32-108(a) uses 'shall petition'. Codified through Public Chapter 608. Untouched by Public Chapters 719, 930 and 1061. Six subsections, (a) through (f), with no further subdivision numbering.

destination.detail: Upon filing, the clerk serves the petition on the district attorney general for that judicial district. Both the petitioner and the district attorney general may file evidence. components.notes: The participant's own operative petition under T.C.A. § 40-32-109(a) for expunction of the participant's arrest record. This is the statutory petition itself, and on this route only it is the participant's document rather than the district attorney general's: § 40-32-109 has no cross-reference to § 40-32-108 and no provision assigning preparation to anyone else. The section prescribes no contents, no verification, no affidavit and no form, so the pleading is drafted to the eligibility condition embedded in (a) — that the court with jurisdiction over the offence for which the person was arrested has no history of the arrest within the court's records — and to the finding the court must make under (d).

Explains the clerk's two statutory duties and that neither is the participant's to perform or pre-empt. Under § 40-32-109(a) the clerk serves the petition on the district attorney general for that judicial district on filing. Under § 40-32-109(c) the clerk's office searches the court's records and certifies to the court whether there is any history of the person's arrest for the offence at issue within the court's records. That certification is neutral in form and is filed either way, because it certifies whether there is any history rather than only a negative. LegalEase does not generate it, does not pre-complete it and does not predict what it will say.

States on the face of the packet that this route is not free. Section 40-32-109(e) provides that a person petitioning the court for expunction pursuant to the section must be charged the appropriate clerk's fee pursuant to T.C.A. § 8-21-401. There is no indigency, waiver or without-cost provision anywhere in § 40-32-109, in express contrast to § 40-32-106(a)(1), which requires qualifying non-conviction records to be removed and destroyed without cost to the person. The amount is not quoted, because the current text of § 8-21-401 sits in the licensed Tennessee Code and was not retrievable from an official Tennessee source.

controllingAuthority.summary: Public Chapter 268 of 2025 split the former § 40-32-101(g) conviction route along an eligibility and procedure seam: § 40-32-107 now defines who is an eligible petitioner and § 40-32-108 supplies the whole procedure. That mapping is officially corroborated rather than inferred — Public Chapter 268's own conforming amendments replaced the old citation to § 40-32-101(g)(3) with § 40-32-107 and the old § 40-32-101(g) with § 40-32-107(a)(1), and replaced procedural references to § 40-32-101 with § 40-32-108. Eligibility under § 40-32-107(a) turns on the offence being on one of the enumerated Class C, Class D or Class E felony lists or within the misdemeanour category subject to its exclusion list, the offence having occurred on or after 1 November 1989 and prior to any conviction for an expunction-ineligible offence including federal and out-of-state offences, no previous expunction under subsection (a), (b) or (c), and fulfilment of every sentence requirement including all fines, restitution, court costs and other assessments, completion of imprisonment or probation, all release conditions, and any required year free from dependency on or abuse of alcohol or a controlled substance. The waiting period at § 40-32-107(a)(3)(B) runs from completion of the sentence: five years for a misdemeanour or Class E felony and ten years for a Class C or Class D felony. Subsection (a)(4) directs the petitioner to § 40-32-108, whose subsection (e) requires the petition and proposed order to be prepared by the office of the district attorney general and given to the petitioner to file. Public Chapter 719, effective 2026-04-14, rewrote the § 40-32-108(d)(2) decision standard, preserving the rebuttable presumption for petitioners eligible under § 40-32-107(a)(1)(A) to (E) while directing the court to weigh the petitioner's interest against the best interests of justice and public safety. destination.detail: Section 40-32-108(e) requires the petition and proposed order to be prepared by the district attorney general's office and given to the petitioner to be filed with the clerk. Both the Tennessee AOC and the TBI direct participants to request a conviction expungement packet from that office. LegalEase generates the participant's request and eligibility record; it does not generate the petition or the order, because those are prosecutor and court instruments.

components.notes: A controlled written request to the office of the district attorney general asking it to prepare the petition and proposed order under T.C.A. § 40-32-108(e). It identifies the convicting court and docket, the offence and its exact statutory section, the date of the offence and of the conviction, the date the sentence was completed, and the statutory basis for eligibility, and it asks for the conviction expungement packet the AOC and TBI both direct participants to request.

A supporting record assembled from the participant's answers and their own documents: the offence mapped to its exact T.C.A. section, the waiting-period computation from completion of the sentence, proof that all fines, restitution, court costs and other assessments are paid, confirmation that any imprisonment or probation is complete and all release conditions met, and the no-other-conviction position from the TBI history. This is what the district attorney's office needs to prepare the petition and what the court reviews under § 40-32-108(d).

Explains the whole chain and who controls each link: the participant requests the packet from the district attorney general; that office prepares the petition and proposed order and gives them to the participant; the participant files with the clerk and pays the clerk's fee under § 8-21-401; the clerk serves the district attorney, who may submit recommendations within 60 days and may file evidence under seal; the court may not order sooner than 61 days after service, must review the TBI certificate required by § 40-32-102(c), and weighs the interest of the petitioner against the best interests of justice and public safety with a rebuttable presumption in favour of a petitioner eligible under § 40-32-107(a)(1)(A) to (E); and on denial no further petition may be filed for two years. Under T.C.A. § 40-32-102(c)(1) the TBI develops a request-for-certification form that is completed by the court and submitted to the TBI before an order of expunction is entered, and under (c)(3) an order must not be entered unless the certificate is attached to it. The TBI determines whether the offence is eligible under § 40-32-107 or § 40-32-105 and notes the determination on the certificate; under (c)(4) the certificate certifies offence eligibility only, not defendant eligibility, and the court retains the duty to determine eligibility. The court is exempt from the certificate requirement for expunctions under § 40-32-109 and § 40-32-106 unless the expunction follows successful completion of pretrial diversion under §§ 40-15-102 to 40-15-107 or judicial diversion under § 40-35-313. This is a court instrument completed by court staff. LegalEase does not generate it, does not complete it and does not assert it has been obtained. A court ordering expunction shall send a copy of the order to the TBI within 30 days for entry into its expunged offender and pretrial diversion database. The order must contain the person's name, date of birth, social security number, the offence dismissed, the state control number referenced in § 8-4-115, the date and cause of dismissal, and the date the order was entered. Nothing changes on a background check until the order reaches the TBI, and the packet tells the participant to confirm that it did.

Runs before any refusal is given, so that a participant this route cannot serve is not told there is no relief when a 2026 route reaches them. Two checks. First, where the conviction is not on the § 40-32-107(a)(1) eligible lists but the participant holds a pardon by the Governor following a positive vote of the board of parole, the participant is evaluated under tn_post_pardon, because T.C.A. § 40-32-107(d) imposes no (a)(1) eligibility requirement and no sentence-completion, waiting-period or predating condition at all. Second, where the participant is refused only because the offence post-dates a conviction under T.C.A. § 55-10-401 and § 40-32-107(a)(3)(A) requires the offence to predate any expunction-ineligible conviction, and the participant has successfully completed a certified recovery court programme and at least ten years separate the DUI conviction from the offence, the participant is evaluated under tn_recovery_court. Neither check changes this route's own eligibility rules; each exists to prevent a false no-relief result.

Subsections (a), (b) and (c) each bar a petitioner previously granted expunction under (a), (b) or (c), and name neither (d) nor (e). Subsection (e)(1)(D) bars a petitioner previously granted expunction under (a), (b), (c) or (e). Subsection (d) states no prior-expunction bar at all and is named by none of the others. AFFECTED TRACKS: tn_eligible_conviction, tn_two_offense, tn_post_pardon, tn_recovery_court and tn_illegal_voting. SCREENING IMPACT: the intake asks whether the participant has previously been granted expunction under (a), (b), (c) or (e) and records the answer, but no screen infers a bar that the subsection under which the participant is applying does not state, and in particular no bar is inferred against or from subsection (d). legalDesignDecision.rationale: Approved as a controlled custom pleading whose artifact is the participant's request to the district attorney general, not the petition. That is the decisive design fact and it comes from the statute: § 40-32-108(e) requires the petition and the proposed order to be prepared by the office of the district attorney general and given to the petitioner to be filed with the clerk. Generating the petition would be generating a prosecutor instrument, which the packet-only model forbids, and generating the TBI expungement order BI-0333 would be generating a court order as a participant assertion, which it also forbids. What is genuinely the participant's is the request for the conviction expungement packet — which both the AOC and the TBI expressly direct participants to make — together with the eligibility record that office needs. Both are generated. The three 2026 overlays are applied to the exact provisions they touch: Public Chapter 719 to the § 40-32-108(d)(2) decision standard, where the rebuttable presumption survives for (a)(1)(A) to (E) petitioners; Public Chapter 930 to the § 40-32-107(a)(1) class lists, with its offence-date limitation applied explicitly and prospectively only; and Public Chapter 1061 recorded as adding a route outside the adopted inventory. No eligibility opinion is asserted: the offence is mapped to its exact section from the judgment, any borderline offence goes to review, and the presumption is described without any statement that the petition will be granted.

controllingAuthority.summary: Read at source on 2026-08-06. Section 40-32-107(b) defines an eligible petitioner as a person seeking expunction of no more than two offences. Each offence must be eligible under § 40-32-107(a)(1) and must have occurred prior to any conviction for an expunction-ineligible offence, including ineligible federal and other-state convictions. The permitted combinations are exhaustive: two misdemeanours, or one felony and one misdemeanour. Two felonies are not available on this route. At filing there must be five years since completion of sentence for any misdemeanour or Class E felony being expunged and ten years for any Class C or Class D felony being expunged, every sentence requirement must be fulfilled for each offence, and the person must not previously have been granted expunction under subsection (a), this subsection (b) or subsection (c). Subsection (b)(2) provides a single-episode merger mirroring (a)(1)(F): contemporaneous same-location single-intent convictions count as a single offence for the purposes of the two-offence limit, so one episode does not consume both slots. Subsection (b)(3) directs the petitioner to § 40-32-108, so the same DA-prepared petition procedure applies. The reciprocal bars across (a), (b) and (c) are lifetime, which is why using this pathway forecloses a later second use and makes the timing decision consequential.

destination.detail: Section 40-32-108(e) requires the petition and proposed order to be prepared by the district attorney general's office and given to the petitioner to be filed with the clerk. Both the Tennessee AOC and the TBI direct participants to request a conviction expungement packet from that office. LegalEase generates the participant's request and eligibility record; it does not generate the petition or the order, because those are prosecutor and court instruments.

components.notes: A controlled written request to the office of the district attorney general asking it to prepare the petition and proposed order under T.C.A. § 40-32-108(e). It identifies the convicting court and docket, the offence and its exact statutory section, the date of the offence and of the conviction, the date the sentence was completed, and the statutory basis for eligibility, and it asks for the conviction expungement packet the AOC and TBI both direct participants to request.

A supporting record assembled from the participant's answers and their own documents: the offence mapped to its exact T.C.A. section, the waiting-period computation from completion of the sentence, proof that all fines, restitution, court costs and other assessments are paid, confirmation that any imprisonment or probation is complete and all release conditions met, and the no-other-conviction position from the TBI history. This is what the district attorney's office needs to prepare the petition and what the court reviews under § 40-32-108(d).

Explains the whole chain and who controls each link: the participant requests the packet from the district attorney general; that office prepares the petition and proposed order and gives them to the participant; the participant files with the clerk and pays the clerk's fee under § 8-21-401; the clerk serves the district attorney, who may submit recommendations within 60 days and may file evidence under seal; the court may not order sooner than 61 days after service, must review the TBI certificate required by § 40-32-102(c), and weighs the interest of the petitioner against the best interests of justice and public safety with a rebuttable presumption in favour of a petitioner eligible under § 40-32-107(a)(1)(A) to (E); and on denial no further petition may be filed for two years. Under T.C.A. § 40-32-102(c)(1) the TBI develops a request-for-certification form that is completed by the court and submitted to the TBI before an order of expunction is entered, and under (c)(3) an order must not be entered unless the certificate is attached to it. The TBI determines whether the offence is eligible under § 40-32-107 or § 40-32-105 and notes the determination on the certificate; under (c)(4) the certificate certifies offence eligibility only, not defendant eligibility, and the court retains the duty to determine eligibility. The court is exempt from the certificate requirement for expunctions under § 40-32-109 and § 40-32-106 unless the expunction follows successful completion of pretrial diversion under §§ 40-15-102 to 40-15-107 or judicial diversion under § 40-35-313. This is a court instrument completed by court staff. LegalEase does not generate it, does not complete it and does not assert it has been obtained. A court ordering expunction shall send a copy of the order to the TBI within 30 days for entry into its expunged offender and pretrial diversion database. The order must contain the person's name, date of birth, social security number, the offence dismissed, the state control number referenced in § 8-4-115, the date and cause of dismissal, and the date the order was entered. Nothing changes on a background check until the order reaches the TBI, and the packet tells the participant to confirm that it did.

Runs before any refusal is given, so that a participant this route cannot serve is not told there is no relief when a 2026 route reaches them. Two checks. First, where the conviction is not on the § 40-32-107(a)(1) eligible lists but the participant holds a pardon by the Governor following a positive vote of the board of parole, the participant is evaluated under tn_post_pardon, because T.C.A. § 40-32-107(d) imposes no (a)(1) eligibility requirement and no sentence-completion, waiting-period or predating condition at all. Second, where the participant is refused only because the offence post-dates a conviction under T.C.A. § 55-10-401 and § 40-32-107(a)(3)(A) requires the offence to predate any expunction-ineligible conviction, and the participant has successfully completed a certified recovery court programme and at least ten years separate the DUI conviction from the offence, the participant is evaluated under tn_recovery_court. Neither check changes this route's own eligibility rules; each exists to prevent a false no-relief result.

participantInputs.question: Which court handled the case, and in which county? A separate filing is needed in each county where you have a case.
What is the docket or case number?
What was the charge, and exactly how did the case end?
On what date did the case end?
What is the state control number on your TBI criminal history? The expunction order cannot be completed without it.
List every other conviction you have anywhere, including federal and out-of-state.
Are you asking about this because of immigration, federal employment or a security clearance? Tennessee expunction does not reach federal records.
What is the exact T.C.A. section you were convicted under? The offence name and class are not enough — Tennessee's eligible lists are section by section.
On what date was the offence committed? This matters independently of the conviction date, because a 2026 change applies only to offences committed on or after 1 July 2026.
Did the conviction occur on or after 1 November 1989?
On what date did you finish the entire sentence — including any imprisonment or probation, all release conditions, and every fine, restitution amount, court cost and other assessment?
Is every fine, restitution amount, court cost and other assessment paid in full? Anything outstanding means the sentence is not complete and the clock has not started.

Have you ever had a conviction expunged in Tennessee before under T.C.A. § 40-32-107(a), (b), (c) or (e)? This route is available once in a lifetime and a previous grant under (a), (b) or (c) closes it. A grant under (e) is recorded because the statute is asymmetric on the point, and no bar is applied against you that the subsection does not state.
Did you hold a commercial driver licence at the time, and did the offence involve a controlled substance or a commercial motor vehicle?
Did your sentence require a period free from dependency on or abuse of alcohol or a controlled substance? If so, have you met at least one year of it?
How many offences are you asking to clear? The limit is two.
Are the two offences both misdemeanours, or one felony and one misdemeanour? Two felonies cannot be done on this route.
Did the offences happen at the same time and place as part of one continuous incident with a single intent? If so they may count as one, leaving your second slot open.
This pathway can be used once in your life. Do you have any other conviction that might become eligible later? Using it now closes the door on that.
Have you received a pardon from the Governor for this conviction? If you have, a different route may reach it even where this one cannot.

If a DUI conviction is what is standing in the way: have you successfully completed a certified recovery court programme, and did the offence you want cleared happen at least ten years after that DUI conviction?

controllingAuthority.summary: Expunction of the conviction record. Under T.C.A. § 40-32-110 the petitioner is entitled to have all public records of the expunged conviction destroyed in the manner set out in the chapter, restoring the person in contemplation of law to the status occupied before arrest, indictment, information, trial and conviction. A person convicted of illegal registration or voting under T.C.A. § 2-19-107, where fifteen years have elapsed since completion of the sentence, every sentence requirement has been fulfilled, the offence occurred prior to any conviction for an expunction-ineligible offence, and the person has not previously been granted expunction under § 40-32-107(a), (b) or (c). The fifteen-year wait is the longest in the chapter — three times the misdemeanour and Class E felony period and half again the Class C and D felony period — and it attaches to a single named offence rather than to an offence class. Codified through Public Chapter 608 and untouched by Public Chapters 719, 930 and 1061. Subsection (c) is not reached by the § 40-32-108(d)(2) rebuttable presumption, which is keyed only to petitioners eligible under § 40-32-107(a)(1)(A) to (E), so no presumption applies and the court weighs the interest of the petitioner against the best interests of justice and public safety.

exclusions: Any conviction other than a violation of T.C.A. § 2-19-107. The subsection reaches that one named offence and no other elections or fraud provision.

A person previously granted expunction under T.C.A. § 40-32-107(a), (b) or (c) for another criminal offence. Subsection (c)(1)(D) names exactly those three and does not name subsection (d).
Restoration of voting rights. That is a separate remedy under separate machinery and is not what expunction under this subsection does.

components.notes: A controlled written request from the participant to the office of the district attorney general for the judicial district of the convicting court, asking that office to prepare the statutory petition and proposed order under T.C.A. § 40-32-108(e). It identifies the convicting court and docket, the offence and its exact statutory section, and the statutory basis relied on. On this route it states that the conviction was under T.C.A. § 2-19-107 and that fifteen years have elapsed since completion of the sentence. This request is the participant's document. It is not the petition and it is not the proposed order.

A controlled eligibility record assembled from the participant's own answers and their own documents, supplied to the district attorney general's office so that it has what it needs to prepare the petition and proposed order, and so that the court has what it reviews under § 40-32-108(d). On this route it carries the § 2-19-107 identification from the judgment, the sentence-completion date and proof that every financial obligation is satisfied, the fifteen-year computation, and the no-other-conviction position from the TBI history. LegalEase states facts the participant supplies; it certifies nothing and determines nothing.

Explains the chain and who controls each link: the participant sends the request; the office of the district attorney general prepares the petition and the proposed order and gives them to the participant; the participant files them with the clerk of the convicting court and pays the clerk's fee under T.C.A. § 8-21-401; the clerk serves the district attorney general, who may submit recommendations within 60 days and may file evidence under seal; the court may not order sooner than 61 days after service and must review the TBI certificate required by § 40-32-102(c) before ruling; and on denial no further petition may be filed for two years under § 40-32-108(d)(3). States plainly that LegalEase does not obtain the district attorney general's agreement, does not negotiate with that office, does not prepare or sign its petition or proposed order, does not create the TBI certificate or the TBI expungement order, makes no judicial finding, certifies no eligibility and promises neither filing nor relief. It also states that subsection (c) carries no rebuttable presumption, and that expunction under this subsection is not restoration of voting rights.

controllingAuthority.summary: Expunction of the pardoned conviction record, with the § 40-32-110 effect. The pardon by itself does not clear the record; it opens this route. A person who received a pardon from the Governor following a positive vote of the Board of Parole recommending it, who petitions the convicting court, and whose conviction the judge finds was not for one of seven enumerated felonies, or an attempt, conspiracy, facilitation or solicitation to commit one of them: first degree murder under § 39-13-202; second degree murder under § 39-13-210; especially aggravated kidnapping under § 39-13-305; aggravated child abuse under § 39-15-402; especially aggravated robbery under § 39-13-403; commission of an act of terrorism under § 39-13-805; or a sexual offence for which the offender must register as a sexual offender or violent sexual offender under chapter 39, part 2 of title 40, or any sexual offence involving a minor. Codified through Public Chapter 608 and then amended by Public Chapter 719, effective 2026-04-14. Public Chapter 719 Section 1 deleted from § 40-32-107(d)(1) the language 'was convicted of a nonviolent crime if the person', and Section 2 deleted and substituted § 40-32-107(d)(1)(A), replacing an open-textured judicial finding that the offence was a nonviolent crime with a closed list of excluded felonies. Public Chapter 719 Section 3 rewrote § 40-32-108(d)(2). Confirmed from the enacted text and material to the design: subsection (d) contains no waiting period, no sentence-completion checklist, no no-prior-expunction bar and no requirement that the offence predate a conviction for an expunction-ineligible offence. Those conditions appear in subsections (b) and (c) but not in (d). Its three requirements at (d)(1)(A), (B) and (C) are cumulative and exhaustive: the judicial finding against the seven-item exclusion list, a positive vote from the board of parole to receive a pardon, and receipt of a pardon by the governor. The eligibility screen for this route must therefore not import the (a) or (c) conditions, which would wrongly refuse petitioners the statute admits. Public Chapter 719 Section 3 rewrote § 40-32-108(d)(2) so that the court weighs the interest of the petitioner against the best interests of justice and public safety; the rebuttable presumption that the petition should be granted is preserved only for petitioners eligible under § 40-32-107(a)(1)(A) to (E). A subsection (d) petitioner therefore gets no presumption, and the court instead considers whether the offence sought to be expunged was violent and any other relevant factors presented by the petitioner and the district attorney general. Violence moved from a jurisdictional bar to a merits consideration.

components.notes: A controlled written request from the participant to the office of the district attorney general for the judicial district of the convicting court, asking that office to prepare the statutory petition and proposed order under T.C.A. § 40-32-108(e). It identifies the convicting court and docket, the offence and its exact statutory section, and the statutory basis relied on. On this route it states that a pardon was received by the Governor following a positive vote of the board of parole, and identifies the conviction so the judge can make the § 40-32-107(d)(1)(A) finding against the seven-item exclusion list. This request is the participant's document. It is not the petition and it is not the proposed order.

A controlled eligibility record assembled from the participant's own answers and their own documents, supplied to the district attorney general's office so that it has what it needs to prepare the petition and proposed order, and so that the court has what it reviews under § 40-32-108(d). On this route it carries the pardon documentation, the board of parole record of the positive vote, and the conviction identification from the judgment. It carries no sentence-completion checklist, no predating statement and no prior-expunction assertion, because subsection (d) imposes none of those and importing them would wrongly narrow the route. LegalEase states facts the participant supplies; it certifies nothing and determines nothing.

Explains the chain and who controls each link: the participant sends the request; the office of the district attorney general prepares the petition and the proposed order and gives them to the participant; the participant files them with the clerk of the convicting court and pays the clerk's fee under T.C.A. § 8-21-401; the clerk serves the district attorney general, who may submit recommendations within 60 days and may file evidence under seal; the court may not order sooner than 61 days after service and must review the TBI certificate required by § 40-32-102(c) before ruling; and on denial no further petition may be filed for two years under § 40-32-108(d)(3). States plainly that LegalEase does not obtain the district attorney general's agreement, does not negotiate with that office, does not prepare or sign its petition or proposed order, does not create the TBI certificate or the TBI expungement order, makes no judicial finding, certifies no eligibility and promises neither filing nor relief. It also states that a subsection (d) petitioner receives no rebuttable presumption, and that under the § 40-32-108(d)(2) text Public Chapter 719 substituted the court considers, in weighing the best interests of justice and public safety, whether the offence sought to be expunged was violent and any other relevant factors presented by the petitioner and the district attorney general.

participantInputs.question: Which court convicted you, in which county, and which judicial district is that?
What is the docket or case number?
What is the exact T.C.A. section you were convicted under? It is tested against a closed list of seven excluded felonies.
Have you received a pardon from the Governor, and on what date?
Did the board of parole return a positive vote to receive a pardon, and on what date?
Was the conviction for an attempt, conspiracy, facilitation or solicitation to commit an offence? The exclusion list reaches those forms expressly.
Was the offence a sexual offence requiring registration as a sexual offender or violent sexual offender, or any sexual offence involving a minor?

In your own words, is there anything you want the court to know about whether the offence was violent? After the 2026 amendment this is something the court weighs rather than a bar, and it is your account to give.
Have you ever been granted an expunction before under T.C.A. § 40-32-107(a), (b), (c) or (e)? Subsection (d) states no bar of its own, so this is recorded rather than applied against you.
What is the state control number on your TBI criminal history?

unresolvedQuestions.question: The prior-expunction bars across the T.C.A. § 40-32-107 subsections are asymmetric on the enacted text and the asymmetry cannot be resolved from it. Subsections (a), (b) and (c) each bar a petitioner previously granted expunction under (a), (b) or (c), and name neither (d) nor (e). Subsection (e)(1)(D) bars a petitioner previously granted expunction under (a), (b), (c) or (e). Subsection (d) states no prior-expunction bar at all and is named by none of the others. AFFECTED TRACKS: tn_post_pardon, tn_recovery_court, tn_illegal_voting, tn_eligible_conviction and tn_two_offense. SCREENING IMPACT: the intake asks whether the participant has previously been granted expunction under (a), (b), (c) or (e) and records the answer, but no screen infers a bar that the subsection under which the participant is applying does not state, and in particular no bar is inferred against or from subsection (d). CURRENT PACKET TREATMENT: the packet reports the participant's own answer and states which bars the governing subsection actually contains; it asserts no conclusion about a subsection that is silent, and it does not tell a participant that a route is closed on the strength of a bar the statute does not impose. REQUIRED FUTURE CLARIFICATION: a statutory amendment naming the subsections reciprocally, or a counsel determination on whether a prior (e) grant closes (a), (b) and (c) and on whether any prior grant closes (d). RUNTIME EFFECT: none. Every Tennessee route is runtime-disabled and none can be served to a participant, so the open question governs release readiness and screening copy rather than anything a participant can reach today.

provenance.sourceStatement: The prior-expunction bars across the § 40-32-107 subsections are asymmetric on the enacted text, and the asymmetry is reported rather than resolved because it cannot be resolved from the text. On the face of the text a prior (e) grant bars a later (e) petition and, by (e)(1)(D), is itself barred by a prior (a), (b) or (c) grant — but (a), (b) and (c) do not name (e), so whether a prior (e) grant closes them is unresolved. Subsection (d) is outside every bar in both directions. This is carried as a release blocker on Routes 2 and 3 and on the two existing conviction tracks, and no screening question asserts a conclusion about it.

legalDesignDecision.rationale: Added by the integrated Tennessee 2026 route inventory decision record. It is the widest of the four additions and the only one Public Chapter 719 touches, and it reaches a population no other Tennessee route can: because subsection (d) imposes no § 40-32-107(a)(1) eligibility requirement, it reaches pardoned convictions that are permanently ineligible under every other subsection. Two design constraints follow directly from the enacted text and both are load-bearing. First, the eligibility screen deliberately imports nothing from subsections (b) or (c): subsection (d) states no waiting period, no sentence-completion checklist, no prior-expunction bar and no requirement that the offence predate an ineligible conviction, and importing any of them would wrongly refuse petitioners the statute admits. Second, violence is not an eligibility bar on this route. Public Chapter 719 replaced the open-textured nonviolent-crime finding with a closed seven-item exclusion list and moved violence into the § 40-32-108(d)(2) merits weighing, so the packet screens the seven categories and prompts the participant's own account on violence without arguing it. The strategy is custom_pleading and the artifact is the participant's request to the district attorney general and their controlled eligibility record; the petition and proposed order remain that office's instruments under § 40-32-108(e) and are never generated or portrayed as LegalEase's own.

controllingAuthority.summary: Expunction of one otherwise-eligible offence, with the § 40-32-110 effect. It does not expunge the DUI. A person seeking expunction of an offence that is eligible for expunction under § 40-32-107(a)(1) and that occurred at least ten years after the person's conviction for an offence under T.C.A. § 55-10-401; who has fulfilled all requirements of the sentence for the offence being expunged, including payment of all fines, restitution, court costs and other assessments, completion of any term of imprisonment or probation, and meeting all conditions of supervised or unsupervised release; who has successfully completed a certified recovery court programme established under title 16; who has not previously been granted expunction under subsection (a), (b), (c) or (e); and who has not been convicted under § 55-10-401 more than one time. This is a relief-from-the-DUI-bar route, not a DUI-expunction route, and reading it the other way would be the single most damaging error available on it. A DUI under § 55-10-401 is itself expunction-ineligible and appears in the § 40-32-107(a)(1)(D) misdemeanour exclusion list, and § 40-32-107(e)(3) provides that a court shall not grant an expunction under the subsection if the offence sought to be expunged involves a motor vehicle and the use of alcohol or a controlled substance, including but not limited to a violation of § 55-10-401. What subsection (e) does is let a person who carries one DUI conviction expunge a different, otherwise-eligible offence committed at least ten years after it — relief that § 40-32-107(a)(3)(A) would otherwise deny, because that provision requires the offence to have occurred prior to any conviction for an expunction-ineligible offence. Added in its entirety by Public Chapter 1061, the Recovery Court Renewal Act, SB1232 / HB1346, effective 2026-07-01. Public Chapter 1061 Section 3 provides that the act takes effect July 1, 2026, the public welfare requiring it, and — unlike Public Chapter 930 — imposes no offence-date limitation, so it applies on its effective date to qualifying petitioners regardless of when the offence was committed. Subsection (e) is not named in the § 40-32-108(d)(2) rebuttable presumption, which reaches only petitioners eligible under § 40-32-107(a)(1)(A) to (E), and it is not reached by the violence-weighing sentence Public Chapter 719 added for subsection (d) petitioners. An (e) petitioner therefore falls into the bare default: the court weighs the interest of the petitioner against the best interests of justice and public safety.

exclusions: The DUI itself. Subsection (e)(3) provides that a court shall not grant an expunction under the subsection if the offence sought to be expunged involves a motor vehicle and the use of alcohol or a controlled substance, including but not limited to a violation of T.C.A. § 55-10-401. This route does not expunge a DUI and must never be described as doing so.
Any offence sought to be expunged that involves a motor vehicle and the use of alcohol or a controlled substance, which is an absolute bar under (e)(3) even where every other condition is met.
Any offence that is not itself eligible for expunction under T.C.A. § 40-32-107(a)(1), which subsection (e)(1)(A)(i) independently requires.
Any offence that did not occur at least ten years after the person's conviction for an offence under T.C.A. § 55-10-401.
A person convicted under T.C.A. § 55-10-401 more than one time, under (e)(1)(E).
A person who has not successfully completed a certified recovery court programme established under title 16.

Any case where a sentence requirement for the offence being expunged remains unfulfilled, including any unpaid fine, restitution amount, court cost or other assessment, any uncompleted term of imprisonment or probation, or any unmet condition of supervised or unsupervised release.
A person previously granted expunction under T.C.A. § 40-32-107(a), (b), (c) or (e), under (e)(1)(D).

waitingPeriods.duration: The offence being expunged must have occurred at least ten years after the person's conviction for an offence under T.C.A. § 55-10-401. This is an interval between two events rather than a wait from sentence completion.

All requirements of the sentence for the offence being expunged must be fulfilled: every fine, restitution amount, court cost and other assessment paid, any term of imprisonment or probation completed, and all conditions of supervised or unsupervised release met.
Successful completion of a certified recovery court programme established under title 16.
The court may not order sooner than 61 days after the petition is served on the district attorney general, who has 60 days to submit recommendations.

geography.venue: The convicting court, under § 40-32-108(a). The request goes to the district attorney general for that judicial district. A person with convictions in more than one judicial district deals with each separately.

destination.name: The office of the district attorney general for the judicial district of the convicting court, then the clerk of that court
destination.detail: Once the district attorney general's office prepares the petition and proposed order, the petitioner files them with the clerk of the convicting court under § 40-32-108(a) and pays the clerk's fee under T.C.A. § 8-21-401. The generated artifact on this route is the participant's own controlled written request to the office of the district attorney general, together with the participant's controlled eligibility record. It is not the statutory petition and it is not the proposed order: T.C.A. § 40-32-108(e) requires both of those to be prepared by the office of the district attorney general and given to the petitioner to be filed with the clerk. LegalEase does not draft, complete, sign or hold out either instrument as its own, and does not make the district attorney general's legal determination.

components.notes: A controlled written request from the participant to the office of the district attorney general for the judicial district of the convicting court, asking that office to prepare the statutory petition and proposed order under T.C.A. § 40-32-108(e). It identifies the convicting court and docket, the offence and its exact statutory section, and the statutory basis relied on. On this route it states that the offence being expunged is eligible under § 40-32-107(a)(1), that it occurred at least ten years after the § 55-10-401 conviction, and that a certified recovery court programme was successfully completed. It asks for expunction of that offence and of no other, and it does not ask for expunction of the DUI. This request is the participant's document. It is not the petition and it is not the proposed order.

A controlled eligibility record assembled from the participant's own answers and their own documents, supplied to the district attorney general's office so that it has what it needs to prepare the petition and proposed order, and so that the court has what it reviews under § 40-32-108(d). On this route it carries the recovery court completion record, the § 55-10-401 judgment that fixes the date the ten-year interval runs from, the judgment for the offence being expunged, and proof that every sentence requirement for that offence is fulfilled. LegalEase states facts the participant supplies; it certifies nothing and determines nothing.

Explains the chain and who controls each link: the participant sends the request; the office of the district attorney general prepares the petition and the proposed order and gives them to the participant; the participant files them with the clerk of the convicting court and pays the clerk's fee under T.C.A. § 8-21-401; the clerk serves the district attorney general, who may submit recommendations within 60 days and may file evidence under seal; the court may not order sooner than 61 days after service and must review the TBI certificate required by § 40-32-102(c) before ruling; and on denial no further petition may be filed for two years under § 40-32-108(d)(3). States plainly that LegalEase does not obtain the district attorney general's agreement, does not negotiate with that office, does not prepare or sign its petition or proposed order, does not create the TBI certificate or the TBI expungement order, makes no judicial finding, certifies no eligibility and promises neither filing nor relief. It also states in terms that this route does not expunge the DUI, that subsection (e)(3) forbids expunging any offence involving a motor vehicle and the use of alcohol or a controlled substance, and that an (e) petitioner receives neither the (a)(1)(A) to (E) rebuttable presumption nor the subsection (d) violence-weighing direction and falls into the bare statutory default.

participantInputs.question: Which court convicted you of the offence you want cleared, in which county, and which judicial district is that?
What is the docket or case number for that offence?
What is the exact T.C.A. section of the offence you want cleared? It has to be on the § 40-32-107(a)(1) eligible lists in its own right.
Does the offence you want cleared involve a motor vehicle together with alcohol or a controlled substance? If it does, this route is closed for it.
How many convictions do you have under T.C.A. § 55-10-401 for driving under the influence? More than one closes this route.
What is the date of that DUI conviction? The ten-year interval runs from it.
On what date was the offence you want cleared committed? It must be at least ten years after the DUI conviction.
Did you successfully complete a certified recovery court programme, and on what date?
On what date did you complete the entire sentence for the offence you want cleared?
Is every fine, restitution amount, court cost and other assessment for that offence paid in full?
Have you completed any term of imprisonment or probation for that offence and met every condition of supervised or unsupervised release?
Have you ever been granted an expunction before under T.C.A. § 40-32-107(a), (b), (c) or (e)?
What is the state control number on your TBI criminal history?
Are you hoping to clear the DUI itself? This route cannot do that, and it is important you know before anything is prepared.

rules.filing: Two steps with different actors. The participant sends the request to the office of the district attorney general for the judicial district of the convicting court. That office prepares the petition and the proposed order under T.C.A. § 40-32-108(e) and gives them to the petitioner, who files them with the clerk of the convicting court under § 40-32-108(a). A person with convictions in more than one judicial district deals with each separately.
rules.fees: A clerk's fee applies. T.C.A. § 40-32-108(a) provides that a person applying for expunction of records under the section must be charged the appropriate court clerk's fee pursuant to § 8-21-401. The amount is set by § 8-21-401, whose current text sits in the licensed Tennessee Code and was not retrievable from an official Tennessee source, so no figure is quoted. Public Chapter 719 did not change any fee provision.
rules.feeWaiver: No indigency or fee-waiver provision appears anywhere in the reorganized T.C.A. §§ 40-32-106 through 40-32-110. None is asserted.
rules.notice: The clerk serves the petition on the district attorney general, who may submit recommendations within 60 days with a copy to the petitioner and may file evidence under seal which is confidential and not a public record. The court may not order sooner than 61 days after service.
rules.service: Through the clerk. The participant does not effect service.
rules.participantSignature: The participant signs the request to the district attorney general and, once that office prepares it, the petition it supplies. LegalEase signs nothing.

unresolvedQuestions.question: The prior-expunction bars across the T.C.A. § 40-32-107 subsections are asymmetric on the enacted text and the asymmetry cannot be resolved from it. Subsections (a), (b) and (c) each bar a petitioner previously granted expunction under (a), (b) or (c), and name neither (d) nor (e). Subsection (e)(1)(D) bars a petitioner previously granted expunction under (a), (b), (c) or (e). Subsection (d) states no prior-expunction bar at all and is named by none of the others. AFFECTED TRACKS: tn_recovery_court, tn_post_pardon, tn_illegal_voting, tn_eligible_conviction and tn_two_offense. SCREENING IMPACT: the intake asks whether the participant has previously been granted expunction under (a), (b), (c) or (e) and records the answer, but no screen infers a bar that the subsection under which the participant is applying does not state, and in particular no bar is inferred against or from subsection (d). CURRENT PACKET TREATMENT: the packet reports the participant's own answer and states which bars the governing subsection actually contains; it asserts no conclusion about a subsection that is silent, and it does not tell a participant that a route is closed on the strength of a bar the statute does not impose. REQUIRED FUTURE CLARIFICATION: a statutory amendment naming the subsections reciprocally, or a counsel determination on whether a prior (e) grant closes (a), (b) and (c) and on whether any prior grant closes (d). RUNTIME EFFECT: none. Every Tennessee route is runtime-disabled and none can be served to a participant, so the open question governs release readiness and screening copy rather than anything a participant can reach today.

Subsection (d) is outside every bar in both directions. This is carried as a release blocker on Routes 2 and 3 and on the two existing conviction tracks, and no screening question asserts a conclusion about it.

legalDesignDecision.rationale: Added by the integrated Tennessee 2026 route inventory decision record. This is a route around the DUI-related eligibility bar and it is not a DUI-expunction route, which is the single most damaging thing that could be got wrong on it: subsection (e)(3) forbids expunging any offence involving a motor vehicle and the use of alcohol or a controlled substance, including a violation of T.C.A. § 55-10-401. What the subsection does is let a person carrying one DUI conviction clear a different, otherwise-eligible offence committed at least ten years later, which § 40-32-107(a)(3)(A) would otherwise deny because a DUI is expunction-ineligible. The packet therefore asks directly whether the participant is hoping to clear the DUI and answers that before anything is prepared. Public Chapter 1061 imposes no offence-date limitation, unlike Public Chapter 930, so it applies on its effective date to qualifying petitioners regardless of when the offence was committed; Public Chapter 930 reaches this route only derivatively, because (e)(1)(A)(i) requires the offence to be eligible under (a)(1) and Public Chapter 930 moves burglary within those lists for offences committed on or after 2026-07-01. No presumption is claimed: subsection (e) is named neither in the (a)(1)(A) to (E) presumption nor in the subsection (d) violence-weighing sentence. The strategy is custom_pleading and the artifact is the participant's request to the district attorney general and their controlled eligibility record; the petition and proposed order remain that office's instruments.

controllingAuthority.summary: Section 40-32-105 is the human trafficking victim expunction provision within the reorganized chapter, and its operative status is confirmed by official cross-reference rather than by any secondary profile: new § 40-32-102(c)(2), enacted by Public Chapter 268, directs the TBI to certify whether an offence is eligible for expunction pursuant to § 40-32-107 or § 40-32-105, and new § 40-32-106(c)(1) refers to a trafficking victim applying for expunction relief under § 40-32-105. Public Chapter 268 §§ 11 and 12 amended the section. Its current text could not be retrieved from any official Tennessee source on 2026-08-06, because it was not created or rewritten by any retrievable act and the Tennessee Code is a licensed publication. Its eligibility conditions, filing vehicle and required contents are therefore not established here and none is asserted.

None of the three is printed in the Code Bill extract and none is claimed to be. None is the vehicle for a participant-facing record-clearing route: the record-clearing consequence of completing pretrial diversion lives in Chapter 32 at § 40-32-106(d), not in Chapter 15. legalDesignDecision.rationale: Process guidance is retained on two substantive grounds and on an adopted exclusion, not on the absence of a form or of text. The adopted readiness record marks this mechanism as outside the current self-help scope, which is an exact product-scope exclusion a normalization worker preserves rather than reopens. Independently, both guidance rationales are in the preserved group and both are real here: establishing that an offence was committed as a consequence of being trafficked is a contested evidentiary showing, and presenting it is individualized advocacy in a survivor-sensitive setting. The node is deliberately not deferred, because detect-name-refer does not depend on the unretrievable text: LegalEase can tell a participant that the route exists, where it sits, and who to go to, without stating a single eligibility condition. What is withheld is any description of the mechanism, and that is carried as a release blocker on the governing mechanism rather than a build blocker, because nothing is being built. The section's operative status rests on official cross-references in the enacted text of Public Chapter 268 rather than on the secondary profile the controlling review relied on, which is a source upgrade recorded here.

limitations.statement: Confirm the statutory citation with the county clerk or district attorney general before every filing. Chapter 32 was reorganized by Public Chapter 268 of 2025, effective 2025-04-24, and codified by Public Chapter 608, the 2026 Code Bill, effective 2026-03-25. Clerks and published guidance may still use the pre-reorganization numbering: the Tennessee AOC's own expunction page is titled to say updated information is coming to reflect changes to T.C.A. § 40-32-101 and still reasons from that section, which since 2025-04-24 has been nothing but a definitions section. A generated petition citing the wrong section is a rejection risk either way, so the packet is built to carry the current citation with the superseded one noted, and instructs the participant to confirm before filing.
